title: Parallel query processing: bringing data to each operator
lead: Adding machines helps only when matching tuples reach the right place and no single machine does most of the work.
goals: Compare shared-memory, shared-disk, and shared-nothing architectures.
Choose a partitioning strategy that fits the workload.
Estimate broadcast and shuffle costs, and identify bottlenecks.

sections.title: What is shared, and where does parallelism happen?
sections.html:
A shop's order scan takes too long on one machine. Four machines could each scan a quarter of the orders. But where are the quarters stored, what can each processor access, and how do we combine their answers without losing or duplicating logical rows? Parallel execution must solve those questions while preserving the query's result.

Begin with resources. In shared memory, processors access one RAM address space and coordinate through shared structures. Memory bandwidth and synchronization can become bottlenecks. In shared disk, nodes have private RAM but access common storage; private caches and updates still need coordination, and storage can become the bottleneck. In shared nothing, each node owns CPU, RAM and disk. A node must send messages to obtain another node's data. Capacity is easier to add, but cross-node work pays network and coordination costs.

Now distinguish the work we divide. Running two independent customer queries at once is inter-query parallelism, which can raise throughput, completed queries per second. Dividing one customer's large query is intra-query parallelism, aiming to reduce its latency, elapsed request time.

Inside one query, splitting a scan across workers is intra-operator parallelism. Overlapping different operators is inter-operator parallelism: a filter can process the scan's first rows while later rows are still being read. Independent branches of a bushy plan can also run together. A blocking sort cannot produce its ordered output merely because its scan has started.

The course contrasts closely connected parallel machines with more geographically separated distributed systems where communication failures and costs are harder to ignore. This is its architectural convention, rather than a universal distance rule. Startup, communication and skew prevent assuming that four workers always mean four times the speed.

Try it: three replicas contain the same order. Should a transparent SQL scan return it three times?

No. Replicas are physical copies of one logical row, not three new orders. The system must route and combine work to preserve the logical query result. Data transparency hides physical placement; it does not promise the same latency after relocation.

sections.title: Choosing a partitioning strategy
sections.html:
Suppose Orders has customer_id, date and region. To divide it horizontally, assign each complete row to one logical partition. Three simple rules lead to different lookup behavior.

RuleExample placementConsequence
Round-robinRows 1,4,7,10 at W1; 2,5,8 at W2; 3,6,9 at W3Counts nearly equal; customer lookup cannot infer its destination
Hash(customer_id)h(id) modulo worker countEqual keys meet; one known customer routes directly
Range(date)January at W1, February at W2, March at W3February scan can skip other date ranges

Range boundaries must cover the key space without unintended gaps or overlaps. Hashing does not preserve date order. Round-robin balances row counts only under its stated rule; different row sizes, CPU costs and update frequencies can still create imbalance.

If one customer owns 40% of all orders, hashing customer_id sends that whole hot key to one partition even if distinct keys are spread uniformly. The hash function cannot split one equal key while also promising every equal key stays together. This is data or workload skew.

Replication adds copies; partitioning divides logical data. Replicas of the January shard do not contain February orders. In contrast, copying an entire small Currency table to every worker makes that complete table available for local joins with each Orders partition. Updates to copies still require a consistency policy.

A predicate on a different key generally needs several workers unless a secondary index, directory or another routing mechanism locates it. Choose placement using the expected access pattern, not only total storage size.

Try it: ten equal-sized rows are round-robin balanced, but one row needs 100 times more CPU. Is execution balanced?

No. The counts are 4,3,3, but the worker receiving the expensive row may dominate elapsed time. Compare bytes, processing work and request load separately from row count.

sections.title: Parallel scans, sorts, and hash joins
sections.html:
Use an original scan estimate: 800 GB, four machines, 2 GB/s each. One machine reads for 800/2=400 seconds. With an even split each reads 200 GB, taking 200/2=100 seconds. This ideal estimate excludes startup, network output, contention and skew; it assumes all four can sustain their rates simultaneously. A predicate can skip a whole partition only when placement information proves it has no qualifying rows.

Sorting requires an additional property. Give worker 1 all keys below 100 and worker 2 all keys at least 100. Sort each partition locally, then concatenate worker 1 before worker 2: the ranges guarantee global order. Locally sorting hash partitions and concatenating bucket order does not.

Joins need equal keys to meet. Let R={(20,r1),(75,r2),(130,r3)}, S={(75,s1),(130,s2)}. Range-partition both inputs at 100:

W1: R={(20,r1),(75,r2)}  S={(75,s1)}
    ⋈ → (75,r2,s1)
W2: R={(130,r3)}         S={(130,s2)}
    ⋈ → (130,r3,s2)

If S instead splits at 50, S's key 75 goes to W2 while R's key 75 stays at W1. Local-only joins lose that match. Both sides need the same partition function, mapping and corresponding placement.

A shuffle sends rows over the network to their required destinations. Parallel hash join shuffles both sides by a compatible join-key hash, then performs local joins. One worker may further partition its data for a Grace hash join and use another hash for in-memory buckets. Worker destinations, local disk partitions and memory buckets are different levels; their counts need not agree. Equal join keys need compatible placement at each corresponding stage.

Try it: can locally sorted hash partitions give a global ORDER BY merely by concatenation?

No. Hash destinations do not encode key ranges. Use ordered disjoint ranges and concatenate in range order, or add a global merge/order step. A correct join result and a globally sorted result are separate requirements.

Key takeaway

For local joins to find every match, tuples with the same join key must meet at the same worker. Using the same key name is not enough: both inputs need the same partitioning function, partition mapping, and placement of corresponding partitions.

sections.title: Four join scenarios
sections.html:
The join algorithm from earlier lessons still runs locally. The new question is how to bring every matching pair together. Work through four starting states rather than choosing “distributed join” as if it were one operation.

  1. Small table already fully replicated: join each disjoint Orders partition with its local Currency copy. Combine the local outputs. Do not process each Orders replica as a separate logical partition.
  2. Both inputs already co-partitioned: matching join keys have the same destination and corresponding partitions are colocated. Local joins need no input redistribution.
  3. Wrong placement, one small input: send a complete copy of the small input to each worker. This is a broadcast; workers retain their different partitions of the large input.
  4. Wrong placement, both large: shuffle rows by a common join-key mapping, then join each destination's inputs locally.

Compare two original network estimates. Let R=120 GB, S=1 GB, eight workers. If all S initially sits at one worker, broadcasting needs seven additional 1 GB copies: 7 GB transferred. Every recipient must be able to store and process S; the number alone does not prove broadcast feasible.

For a different shuffle starting state, suppose every row is initially uniformly randomly located. Its target is one of eight workers; probability 1/8 it is already there, 7/8 it moves. Expected transfer is (120+1)×7/8=105.875 GB. This excludes output, headers and protocol overhead. The comparison depends on the stated initial placement, not just table sizes.

Try it: if both tables already have compatible local partitions, should you still charge 105.875 GB?

No. That figure belongs to the random-placement shuffle model. Compatible existing placement avoids that input shuffle. A cost model must describe the plan's actual starting state and required movement.

sections.title: The critical path and data skew
sections.html:
Four scan workers finish in 3,3,3,12 seconds. The phase cannot finish before the fourth worker: at least 12 seconds. The average 5.25 seconds is neither its completion time nor a substitute for waiting at the synchronization boundary.

The slow worker may own more rows, a hot join key, larger records, or slower hardware. First identify the cause. Adding more workers will not split a hot key automatically if the placement rule still sends all of it to one destination. Communication, startup and the coordinator's result collection may become bottlenecks after local CPU work shrinks.

Reduce movement before paying for it. Suppose an Orders scan reads customer_id,date,comment but the join needs only customer_id and a date predicate keeps one month. Applying that predicate before the shuffle drops irrelevant rows; projecting away comment reduces each transmitted row's bytes. Both preserve semantics only if all later-needed fields and rows are retained.

State which metric improves: bytes transferred, total CPU work, throughput, or end-to-end latency. A plan using fewer total operations can still be slower when it concentrates work on one critical worker. Likewise, a faster scan does not guarantee a faster query if the join or final sort dominates.

Try it: two tables are hashed on a column named id. Is a local-only join necessarily complete?

No. Check the actual hash function, partition count/mapping and colocated destinations. R's id=75 and S's id=75 must meet at the same worker. A matching column name does not establish that placement contract. The misaligned range example showed the same failure concretely.

Try it: after adding workers, times are 1,1,1,12 seconds. What is the new phase time?

Still at least 12 seconds. The bottleneck remains on the critical path. Reducing the other workers' time improves some work totals but has not shortened this phase's completion.

Key takeaway

A parallel phase must wait for its slowest worker. Skew concentrates work in one partition. Adding workers may not help if the heavy partition is still assigned to one worker.

quiz.question: Workers take 4, 5, 5, and 15 seconds in one parallel phase. What is the lower bound on the phase duration?
quiz.explanation: The phase must wait for its slowest worker. Coordination and network overhead may increase the total duration further.

source.summary: Lecture 26 compares resource-sharing architectures, levels of parallelism, partitioning and replication, parallel scans, sorts, and joins, and cost models that account for network traffic and skew.
